measure: lowest O2 sustaining opposed-flow flame spread (flow 0.4-8 cm/s)
flag: Burns at lower O2 in space
finding: Flame spread was sustained at lower oxygen in microgravity (17%) than in normal gravity (18%), so the limiting oxygen is lower in space.
source: Link et al. 2018, The Effect of Gravity on Flame Spread over PMMA Cylinders, Scientific Reports (BASS-II)

measure: flame spread rate at low oxygen
flag: Mixed: faster in space below 19% O2
finding: Below 19% O2 flames spread faster in microgravity than in normal gravity; at 21% O2 the order reverses and normal-gravity spread is faster.
source: Link et al. 2018, The Effect of Gravity on Flame Spread over PMMA Cylinders, Scientific Reports (BASS-II)

measure: limiting oxygen for opposed-flow flame spread
flag: Burns at lower O2 in space
finding: On Earth the limiting oxygen index in opposed flow is 16.5%, but at spacecraft-like ventilation (5-20 cm/s) flames can be sustained at 14% O2. A normal-gravity flammability measure does not guarantee a material will not burn in space.
source: Olson 2004, Most Probable Fire Scenarios in Spacecraft and Extraterrestrial Habitats: Why NASA's Current Test 1 Might Not Always Be Conservative, NASA/TM-2004-213114

measure: air flow needed for a flame to survive
finding: Experiments showed a very slight air flow, a fraction of a cm/s, is enough for a flame to survive; such flames can become almost undetectable yet persist for minutes, even after ventilation is turned down.
Microgravity flames preferentially spread upwind (opposed flow), not downwind as in the normal-gravity upward Test 1, so Test 1 may not represent the worst case for spacecraft fires.

measure: burn length in concurrent flow at 20 cm/s and ~21.5% O2
finding: The opposite direction: this silicone sample burned completely in the 1 g test but did not sustain burning in low gravity (burn time recorded as insignificant). Earth-vs-space differences depend on the material.

measure: flame spread in concurrent flow at 20 cm/s and ~22% O2
flag: Burned in both; steadier spread in space
finding: Burned in both cases: in 1 g the spread accelerated and consumed the sample; in low gravity the flame spread at a steady 2.1-2.6 mm/s over the 29 cm sample.

measure: burning after the visible flame goes out (0.5 atm)
finding: In microgravity, large n-alkane droplets kept burning in a low-temperature cool flame after radiative extinction of the visible flame; cameras could not see it, only radiometers. Observed for n-decane between 14% and 21% O2 at 0.5 atm; at 25% O2 radiative extinction was avoided.
source: Nayagam, Dietrich, Hicks, Williams 2014, Cool-flame extinction during n-alkane droplet combustion in microgravity (FLEX)
